title: Decoding pattern repeats
subtitle: What the asterisks, brackets, and parentheses in written patterns actually mean
excerpt: Crochet patterns use asterisks and brackets to mark sections of instructions that repeat. Once you know what each symbol means, a page of abbreviations becomes a clear sequence of actions.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book — pattern notation chapter. Standard British crochet pattern conventions.

glossaryTerms.definition: A pattern section marked with * at the start and a phrase like 'repeat from * to end' or 'repeat from * 3 more times'. Everything between the first asterisk and the end marker repeats the stated number of times.

A pattern section enclosed in square brackets or parentheses with a multiplication note immediately after, e.g. [3 tr, ch 2] 4 times. The contents of the bracket repeat exactly the stated number of times.

heroPrompt: A close-up of a printed crochet pattern page with a single line of abbreviated instructions and one asterisk repeat highlighted in yellow marker, on a pale background.

content.text: A written crochet pattern condenses long sequences of identical actions using notation shorthand. The two most common forms are the
. Both mean "do this section again". They are not interchangeable in a single pattern — read the pattern notes to see which convention the designer is using.

Example: "*1 dc, ch 1, skip 1. Repeat from * to last 2 sts." This means: work [1 dc, ch 1, skip 1] over and over across the row, stopping when only 2 stitches remain. Count the stitches per repeat (here: 3 stitches consumed each time) and check the stitch count at the end of the row to confirm you worked the right number of repeats.

Example: "[3 tr into corner space, ch 2] 4 times." This means: work [3 tr, ch 2] exactly four times in sequence. The bracket repeat is unambiguous about count — no need to calculate how many times to repeat based on row length.

Some patterns have both. Example: "*[1 dc, ch 2, 1 dc] into corner sp, 3 dc across side. Repeat from * 3 more times." Read the bracket first (it's a sub-action within the larger repeat), then the asterisk repeat wraps the whole sequence. Work the inside bracket actions, then the outside repeat.
Stitch counts at the end of a row

After a repeat section, most patterns state the expected stitch count in brackets: e.g. "(48 sts)". Count your stitches when you reach this marker. If your count doesn't match, the repeat count is wrong — too few or too many repeats before the pattern moved to the end stitches. Fix the count before continuing, not after completing several more rows.

attrs.title: Mark your place in a row
attrs.body: For long repeating rows, use a small sticky note under the line you are currently working. Move it down as you finish each row. With complex repeat patterns, also make a tick mark (pencil on paper, or a phone notepad) each time you complete one full repeat — a mis-count on row 30 is much faster to diagnose if you know which repeat you were on.
